findings.where: explain.text and the steps (best placed at step 9 'Going back', or in one closing line of the last SHOW screen)
findings.what: The brief promised a link to phasors in this lesson, and it is missing. No screen or sentence says that a phasor is a complex number for "the magnitude and phase of a voltage or a current" (UTK, notes 6.5). Nothing writes a supply as 230∠0° (example figure). The MCA's 'I cos θ and I sin θ', which splits a phasor into its two components (notes 3.5), is not tied to a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ either. As a result r∠θ is never connected to the AC arrows Dan drew in Trigonometry lessons 6 and 7, and lesson 8 uses 230∠0° as if he already knew it.

findings.where: Step 7 'A whole turn' (more text), and explain.text ('Textbooks add that the usual choice is ... the principal argument')
findings.what: The range of angles is stated with no citation: 'more than −180° and up to 180°, which college texts call the principal argument'. None of the lesson's six sources supports it. The notes have the quotes, so add them as a footnote: HELM, "We normally consider θ ... to lie in the interval −π < θ ≤ π although any value θ + 2kπ ... will be equivalent", and SQA EM1, "noting the domain of principal argument" (notes 4.5).

findings.where: Step 5 'Half a turn out' (more text), and the practice step 'add 180° when the arrow points up, take 180° away when it points down'
findings.what: The lesson never says why it adds 180° in one case and takes it away in the other. Either half turn lands the ghost on the arrow: 53.13° + 180° = 233.13° also names −3 − j4. Taking 180° away just keeps the answer between −180° and 180°, and that range only arrives two screens later, so the rule reads as arbitrary. One clause on step 5 would close the gap, for example 'either half turn lands on the arrow; this way keeps the angle in the usual range'.

findings.where: Step 1 'The length', the 'Length and angle' card
findings.what: The card shows 5∠53.13° from the first frame, two screens before the angle is taught. On this screen, show the length with the angle still unknown (for example '5∠?'), and let step 3 fill in 53.13° when its working arrives.

The screen names the length 'the modulus' but never 'magnitude'. The brief makes magnitude one of the main words, and it is the word in the phasor definition Dan will meet at college. Only explain.text has 'or magnitude', so add those two words to the screen.

findings.where: Step 11 'On the axes' (text, and the −4 half of the demonstration)
findings.what: The text opens with 'An arrow along an axis needs no tan⁻¹ at all', but for −4 the demonstration then draws the calculator's ghost at 0° and the +180° arc, which is the tan⁻¹ route. Say that 180° can be read straight off the sketch for −4, and that the calculator route agrees after the half turn.

findings.where: Step 13 '10∠−36.87° as parts', the angle label (360 px light end state)
findings.what: The label clearer has pushed '−36.87°' up above the real axis, while its arc sits below the axis, so at a glance the label is on the positive side. The arc is also only a small tick at R = 24 px on this scale. Use a larger radius so that the label fits below the axis, beside the arc.

findings.where: interactive.numbers, 'Slip 180 added instead, angle of −1 + j1, in step 5' = 135
findings.what: The label gives the wrong working. Adding 180° to the calculator's 45° makes 225°, not 135°. The 135° answer is 180° − 45°, which is the up-and-left quarter, the slip the step-6 hint actually describes. Relabel it, for example 'Slip wrong quarter, 180° − 45°, the angle of −1 + j1'.

findings.where: explain.text 'It always answers with an angle between −90° and 90°', the shaded half 'tan⁻¹ points here', and numbers 'Calculator tan⁻¹ answers from/up to'
findings.what: The range of the tan⁻¹ key carries the whole explanation, but it is listed as a constant with no source and no reason. Tie it back to Trigonometry lesson 3, where 'the calculator's sin⁻¹ gives only one of them', or cite it, so it is not a bare assertion.

findings.where: interactive.ignores ('a third way of writing r∠θ ... this course does not need it')
findings.what: Lesson 6 will say in one line that HND texts write r∠θ as re^{jθ}. Change 'this course does not need it' to 'lesson 6 names it'. Also, r(cos θ + j sin θ), shown in explain.text, is already a third way of writing it, so 'third' is ambiguous.
The right answer is the middle button in four of the seven puzzles (steps 2, 8, 10 and 12). Move one or two of them so that position gives nothing away.
